items.summary: Unrefereed research candidate. In one sentence: the matrix geometric mean can jump at singular matrices, every possible jump is described by one rank condition, and the same mechanism refutes a published claim that the symbol of the geometric mean of two GLT matrix-sequences is always the geometric mean of their symbols. The geometric mean A#B of two positive definite matrices is the matrix analogue of √(ab), used to average covariance matrices and structured matrices and to define the Matsumoto fidelity of quantum states. It need not be continuous at singular pairs. Theorem 1 shows that X is a limit of A j #B j with positive definite A j → A, B j → B exactly when X ≽ 0, the block matrix [[A, X], [X, B]] is positive semidefinite and its rank is at most the dimension N (a dilation description with an auxiliary contraction already follows from recent work of Jones; the explicit elimination is the contribution). At equal inputs this gives the full set of limits and the exact interval of limiting Matsumoto fidelities. For generalized locally Toeplitz (GLT) matrix-sequences, uniformly bounded positive definite inputs with identical scalar symbols can have geometric means with the wrong symbol (4/5 instead of 1 on half the interval) or no eigenvalue distribution at all. This refutes Theorem 4 and Conjecture 1 of the arXiv version of Ilyas, Khan, Loi and Serra-Capizzano and, according to an AI-assisted reading of the published text, Theorem 3 and Conjecture 1 of their article in Linear Algebra Appl. (2025); the failing step of the proof is located. Positive results: closure for every Kubo-Ando mean when the sum of the symbols is positive definite almost everywhere; a one-sided theorem that the regularised symbol is always an upper envelope; and, for bounded Riemann-integrable scalar symbols of the space variable only, a sharp dichotomy (the formula holds for every realisation if and only if the symbols have no common zero set of positive measure or essentially disjoint supports). The classical two-dimensional discontinuity, Ando's maximal characterisation and the envelope X ≼ A#B are earlier work and are credited. The archive contains the manuscript (PDF and Markdown source), two figures with the script that draws them, an exact verifier (verify_exact.py, Python standard library only, 1,030 rational and Gaussian-rational checks of closed forms and finite assemblies, with a mutation self-test) and its retained output, the bibliography with its Crossref/arXiv records, the dated novelty ledger, a revision note, CI and SHA-256 sums. Assurance: written proofs; the verifier checks finite exact identities, not the theorems' limits or quantifiers; internal AI-assisted review only (not human peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification). Creator: Anonymous. Text and figures CC0-1.0; code MIT.
items.title: Boundary limits of the matrix geometric mean and the failure of unrestricted GLT closure

items.summary: We disprove a three-step error estimate for the Broyden--Fletcher--Goldfarb--Shanno {(BFGS)} method with exact line searches. We construct a globally strongly convex function $F\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and a single nonterminating trajectory $x_k\to0$ for which $\limsup_{k\to\infty}\|x_{k+3}\|/(\|x_{k+2}\|\|x_k\|)=+\infty$. The Hessian of $F$ lies between $\tfrac12 I$ and $\tfrac32 I$ everywhere, and $F(x)-\tfrac12\|x\|^2$ is compactly supported with all derivatives vanishing at $0$. The proof first constructs point-gradient pairs satisfying the exact BFGS step identities. A five-step cycle produces a large three-step quotient and restores an invariant plane for the actual updated matrix, allowing the cycle to be repeated with arbitrarily small gradient errors. Disjoint smooth corrections to a quadratic then realize all the pairs by one objective. Strong convexity identifies the prescribed points with the unique exact line-search minimizers. Thus smoothness and strong convexity do not imply the proposed product estimate, even for an objective that agrees with a quadratic to every order at its minimizer.
items.title: A counterexample to a three-step convergence bound for BFGS with exact line search

items.summary: Support points provide a practical and effective way to approximate a probability distribution by a small set of equally weighted representatives through energy-distance minimization. In many applications, the variables satisfy convex constraints that the representatives should also respect. We investigate whether unconstrained support points automatically satisfy such constraints and show that this is not guaranteed. We construct counterexamples using three planar observations, a density with full triangular support, and positive-definite matrix data admitting an indefinite optimal representative under the Frobenius norm. We also identify cases in which containment holds, establish stability under distributional perturbations, and quantify the objective cost of imposing a convex-hull constraint. For a fixed number of representatives and a positive population constraint gap, empirical configurations with vanishing global objective error eventually leave the sample convex hull almost surely.
items.title: Unconstrained support points can leave a convex support

items.summary: We give a negative answer to a question of Sánchez Saldaña--Velásquez and Lück asking whether the topological K-theory of the reduced group C*-algebra of a split crystallographic group with finite cyclic holonomy is always torsion-free. For two explicit split crystallographic groups with translation subgroup of rank four and holonomy of order four, we compute the equivariant K-theory of the classifying space for proper actions and find nontrivial two-torsion. The equivariant universal coefficient theorem transfers this torsion to proper equivariant K-homology, and the Baum--Connes conjecture identifies the resulting groups with the topological K-theory of the corresponding reduced group C*-algebras.
items.title: Counterexamples to torsion-freeness in the $K$-theory of crystallographic group $C^*$-algebras

items.summary: Overview: This deposit hosts the official replication package, synthetic benchmark dataset, and experimental audit artifacts for the scientific manuscript: "M-11: Auditing Synthetic Risk Labels and Physical Baselines in a Cyber-Physical Benchmark for Underground Mining" (submitted to Acta Montanistica Slovaca , 2026). M-11 is a simulation-only cyber-physical benchmark that integrates AI4I 2020 predictive maintenance attributes with synthetic kinematic positioning, physiological, and environmental indicators (10,000 records; 37 columns) to audit the statistical mechanics and potential circularity of synthetic risk labelling in confined underground mining operations. Key Empirical Findings Reported in the Manuscript: Label Circularity Audit: Variance decomposition demonstrates that 82.07% of the synthetic score variance is driven by spatial/kinematic components, 17.43% by injected noise, 0.48% by multimodal variables, and 0.02% by cross-covariance. Symmetric Holdout Evaluation (n = 2,000; seed 42): Calibrated Time-to-Collision (TTC) and Random Forest both achieve F2 = 0.9103; XGBoost achieves F2 = 0.9065. The paired bootstrap difference (ΔF2 = -0.0038, 95% CI: -0.0129 to 0.0047) and Holm-adjusted McNemar test (p = 0.6015) confirm no statistically significant gap under circular labels. Decoupled Hazard Stress Tests: Under 22% class prevalence and low signal-to-noise ratio, non-spatial decoupled labels (CO, fatigue, vibration) push F2 optimisation to near-universal HIGH alerts, approaching the trivial Always-HIGH baseline (F2 = 0.5851). A multimodal-only composite target recovers F2 = 0.6408 with 54.1% specificity. Feature Ablations: Removing three direct kinematic indicators reduces F2 by 9.60 percentage points; removing the entire 8-feature spatial block reduces F2 by 32.52 percentage points from the full 0.9065 baseline. Computational Scalability: Local backend P95 latency scales to 27.91 ms under 500 concurrent simulated agents (< 200 ms supervisory threshold). The WebGL/Three.js integrated-GPU prototype achieves 34.8 FPS under nominal load. Deterministic Safety & GenAI Audit: The independent deterministic safety layer satisfies 17 automated unit/integration tests and 100/100 scripted regulatory scenario checks. The Gemini language model acts strictly as an exploratory natural-language interface without numerical autonomy. Package Contents & Cryptographic Verification (SHA-256): public_mining_equipment_dataset.csv (3,859,401 bytes) — SHA-256: b71d0b6baed8b6e0bc7eee1a1a5b7440d06a04ddaea5d502907cf03d958705f0 requirements.txt (574 bytes) — Frozen Python 3.10.11 scientific environment specifications. results/feature_dictionary.csv (2,928 bytes) — Full data dictionary defining all 37 attributes, physical units, and provenance. results/label_circularity_audit.json (17,530 bytes) — Machine-readable variance decomposition and baseline comparison exports. results/genai_audit_bank.json (35,882 bytes) — 100 structured synthetic scenarios for LLM compliance auditing. results/genai_audit_review_sheet.csv (47,295 bytes) — Manual verification rubric with inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's κ = 0.85). Boundary of Scope: M-11 is a computational simulation benchmark and exploratory supervisory prototype. It does not establish mine-site functional safety, nor does it claim active-mine physical twin synchronisation or autonomous braking actuation.
items.title: Dataset and Replication Package for M-11: Auditing Synthetic Risk Labels and Physical Baselines in a Cyber-Physical Benchmark for Underground Mining

items.summary: The Sundarbans mangrove system constitutes a globally consequential blue carbon sink, yet vertically resolved soil organic carbon (SOC) inventories, particularly at depth, remain under-constrained. This study deployed a geospatial deep-learning pipeline integrating multi-source Earth observation data (optical, SAR, and DEM-derived covariates) to spatially upscale SOC stocks to 1 m depth across the Bangladesh Sundarbans. Stratified coring across five sites positioned along the salinity–tidal inundation gradient to represent four major vegetation zones (n = 25; one pit per site × five depth intervals: 0–20, 20–40, 40–60, 60–80, 80–100 cm) captured physicochemical and SOC attributions. A Kruskal–Wallis test confirmed a positive SOC gradient with depth (H = 21.7, df = 4, p < 0.001); post-hoc Dunn’s pairwise comparisons showed 60–100 cm layers differed significantly from all shallower layers (p < 0.01, Bonferroni-adjusted), with the dominant pool residing below 40 cm, implying systematic underestimation by conventional shallow-core (<30–40 cm) assessments. To partition total ecosystem carbon and establish soil-pool dominance, above- and belowground biomass were parameterized using species-specific allometric equations, revealing high stem density but comparatively low basal area consistent with a regenerating stand structure dominated by Heritiera fomes and Sonneratia apetala. Analysis of a previously published Landsat-derived mangrove record (1988–2022) revealed net contraction in mangrove extent; loss-agent raster attribution, based on shoreline-proximity buffers, land-cover transition sequences and cyclone-track coincidence, identified chronic tidal abrasion and erosion as the primary driver rather than anthropogenic conversion or cyclonic disturbance. Benchmarking against a previously published global 30 m machine-learning SOC product revealed a 4.2-fold underestimation of SOC stocks in the Bangladesh Sundarbans, particularly in peat-enriched, anoxic substrata. Assimilation of deep-profile in situ observations with the pipeline significantly improves spatial prediction fidelity and establishes a robust baseline for Measurement, Reporting, and Verification for greenhouse gas inventories, highlighting the necessity of incorporating deep-soil carbon pools for inventorizing erosion-vulnerable seaward margins.
items.title: Blue Carbon Stock Mapping of the Sundarbans Mangrove Ecosystem, Bangladesh (2000–2025): A Hybrid GeoAI Ensemble Framework

items.summary: Abstract Sānér establishes a recursive control architecture for task regions by placing topology, self-modeling scheduling, and certificate-governed execution under one executable resource semantics. The nine-node construction supports exact recursive expansion and addressing. Its formal system establishes capacity safety, deterministic cross-layer selection, partition safety, conditional liveness, and computable deadline and recovery bounds. Using entity-isolated validation and one-time test splits, we evaluated the shared kernels and domain adapters in executable state-transition simulations and public benchmark workloads over 32–64 independent worlds, with deployment evidence obtained from 48 physical GPU blocks and eight fresh process pairs in the official Kubernetes scheduler-performance harness. Shared kernels with explicit domain realizations established task-level all-comparator superiority, while matched Kubernetes execution established a throughput advantage over the official default scheduler. The recursive representation preserved exact adjacency with a small measured footprint as graph size increased. Mechanism evidence remains separate from direct performance claims. Boundary results and nonidentifiability tests are reported independently. Together, the proofs and matched comparisons establish Sānér as a reusable and auditable control architecture whose shared mechanisms transfer across structurally different systems tasks. Validation design The study reports 52 simulation tasks and two deployment endpoints. Simulation comparisons use matched frozen worlds, observable information, action spaces, resource ceilings, and decision-time budgets. The Kubernetes deployment uses fresh paired processes under the same official scheduling and binding boundaries. Independent-unit inference, primary endpoints, and comparison procedures follow the recorded experimental contracts. Task-level all-comparator conclusions require passage against every member of the specified comparator family. Suite-defined Holm or FDR adjustments control multiplicity. Direct performance, mechanism validation, boundary results, and nonidentifiability remain separate evidence classes. Comparator strength and field standing Comparator selection was deliberately demanding. The experiments include established scheduling methods, matched MPC and CP-SAT, public MAPF implementations, official Kubernetes scheduling, strong decentralized-learning algorithms, and mature domain-specific methods. Every direct comparison uses matched information and resources. Executed comparator implementations are identified precisely. The consensus experiment uses a HotStuff three-chain simulation and a validation-tuned partition-threshold selector. The distribution-estimation experiment uses a discounted-loss context-depth KT mixture alongside Bayesian online changepoint prediction and discounted KT estimation. Published BFTBrain and context-tree weighting provide the corresponding methodological lineages. Results overview Sānér established task-level all-comparator superiority across 38 simulation tasks. Representative findings include a 764.53% improvement over equal-degree expander control, a 208.90% improvement over Exact Diffusion, and a 33.40% improvement over the Graph500 top-down port. At 5,000 nodes, the topology-based placement adapter sustained 69,258 placements per second. Under matched official Kubernetes execution, Sānér achieved 892.80 placements per second versus 371.19 for the default scheduler, with a mean paired throughput ratio of 2.40. Exact recursive-topology representation preserved neighbor recovery at 508–716 measured bytes through 26,244 nodes. Complete self-modeling was measured independently. The full experimental result index is provided in the Additional Description. Confirmatory scope The 38 task-level conclusions cover their complete specified strong-comparator families. items.summary: Rapid advances in cowork agents are shifting human-AI collaboration toward real-world automation, delivering software, designs, and other artifacts. However, such productivity work demands both high-quality delivery on complex productivity tasks and continued monitoring and decision-making over long horizons, a combination that remains an open challenge. We introduce CoworkOS, a general-purpose harness for long-horizon work that separates task strategy from execution management: the model decides actions, delegation, and acceptance, while the runtime maintains state and feedback. Its three-layer architecture enables direct execution or delegation to Subagents, synchronously or asynchronously, under stable responsibilities. Through a shared application layer, humans and agents inspect and revise the same evolving documents, presentations, CAD models, and Blender scenes, so human-in-the-loop participation can enter both through conversation and through direct modification of the work itself. To sustain continuity across agents and sessions, CoworkOS further introduces hierarchical workspaces and persistent semantic memory, so working files, key decisions, and long-running Job logs remain shareable, reusable, and resumable after interruption. Across 12 benchmarks and 6 categories of real-world applications, CoworkOS proves highly competitive with frontier agent applications such as Codex and DeepSeek Harness. As a sustained-work case study, CoworkOS uses GLM-5.3 as its backbone to conduct RSI-driven automated post-training on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Over five rounds, the model's average score across eight benchmarks rose from 33.19 to 42.95 (+9.76). Looking ahead, we believe CoworkOS opens a meaningful path toward general cowork-agent intelligence.
items.title: CoworkOS:Scaling Agent Coworkers for Real-world Automation

items.summary: The Neptunian desert and savanna are separated by a ridge, an overdensity at orbital periods of approximately 3-6 d identified with Kepler. Like the hot Jupiter pileup at larger radii, this feature has been linked to the accumulation of successful outcomes of high-eccentricity migration (HEM). We revisit the ridge independently using TESS occurrence posteriors for FGK main-sequence stars. We quantify its excess over adjacent regions and compare six occurrence profiles using leave-one-out cross-validation and Bayesian evidence. For planets with radii of approximately 5-8 $R_\oplus$, the ridge has twice the occurrence density of the denser neighbouring region ($J=2.05^{+0.52}_{-0.44}$), with 99.9% posterior support (one-sided Gaussian equivalent of $3.1σ$). This contrast agrees with the discovery study and earlier Kepler occurrence measurements. Both predictive performance and Bayesian evidence strongly favour profiles peaking within the ridge over a single power law. The lognormal is preferred, suggesting a narrower inner wing and a more extended outer wing, although evidence for asymmetry remains weak. In the same period window, the analysis recovers the hot Jupiter pileup (approximately 10-16 $R_\oplus$) with a contrast consistent with that of the ridge and excludes an analogous excess among sub-Neptunes (approximately 2-4 $R_\oplus$) with $3.4σ$ posterior support. TESS thus provides an independent detection of the Neptunian ridge. Its possible asymmetry would be compatible with HEM, in which tidal disruption could produce a sharper inner edge and variations in circularisation efficiency a more gradual outer decline. Establishing whether the ridge has this shape requires more precise occurrence measurements, with PLATO's expected planet yield offering a promising opportunity to help unveil its morphology.
items.title: The Neptunian ridge through the lens of TESS

items.summary: LLM agents repeatedly send a growing conversation to a model, making prefix reuse central to efficient serving. We show that a brief surge can disrupt this reuse and trigger metastable failure in prefill--decode (PD) disaggregated engines: service remains degraded after arrivals return to a load the engine previously sustained. On SGLang, a ten-minute surge reduced goodput by about 88% over the following hour. Removing the residual burst sessions restored service within minutes. The sustaining mechanism is population-cache feedback. Slower calls prolong sessions and enlarge their aggregate context, or working set; the resulting cache misses increase recomputation and further delay departures. A fluid model identifies the resource conditions for this feedback and explains how cache capacity, tool time and base load affect vulnerability. Across 36 simulated deployments, it flags all 17 cache-first cases. Controlled simulations hold the post-surge state fixed and show that changing subsequent arrivals alone reverses the recovery outcome. Once the cache collapses, low-reuse departure capacity sets the scale of the load reduction needed for recovery. Guided by these dynamics, we build Basin, which gives each session a fixed priority, reserves their predicted peak contexts against an adaptive admission budget, extends the cache with idle decode memory, and sheds excess demand. On real H200 1P3D deployments under surges, including long-context SWE-bench Pro sessions, an arrival-time prototype achieves 1.20--1.70x the goodput of Continuum and 2.35--3.59x that of HiCache alone. In simulation, the predictor-driven policy delivers 1.20--2.05x the strongest baseline's goodput across six surge scenarios.
items.title: When Cache Pressure Becomes a Trap: Metastability in Agent Serving

items.summary: One way to compare two graphs $G_1, G_2$ is to check whether there is some graph $H$ in a graph class $\mathcal{H}$, such that the number of homomorphisms from $H$ to $G_1$ is not equal to that from $H$ to $G_2$. This is the field of homomorphism distinguishability which has gained a lot of traction in recent years. In this paper, we study the case where $\mathcal{H}$ is the class of graphs of treewidth $k$. This has connections to important concepts in logic, machine learning, combinatorial optimization and proof complexity. In particular, Dvořák showed that $G_1$ and $G_2$ can be distinguished by a homomorphism count from a graph of treewidth $k$ iff $G_1$ and $G_2$ are distinguishable by the $k$-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm. While the relation between the iteration number of this algorithm and the depth of the tree-decomposition of a distinguishing graph is understood, our understanding of the \emph{size} of $H$ is limited. We show a $2^{Ω(n^{k/2})}$ lower bound on the size of a graph of treewidth $k$ required to distinguish two graphs of order $n$. This bound is proved via a new combinatorial game along with a construction which uses a recent compression technique for CFI graphs. It is almost tight to the known $2^{O(n^{k+1})}$ upper bound and is an exponential improvement on the previous best known lower bound.
items.title: An Almost-tight Size Lower Bound for Bounded Treewidth Homomorphism-Distinguishability

items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate detailed video captions, yet they may overemphasize minor details while overlooking essential context and key events. We argue that not all visual evidence deserves equal attention, as the importance of visual information depends on the content of each video. Motivated by this observation, we propose Reviso, an agentic video captioning framework that learns what to observe and how to gather relevant visual evidence. From a low-frame-rate global preview, Reviso constructs a hierarchical Context--Focus--Points (CFP) observation plan that identifies the video context, prioritizes key aspects, and defines concrete observation targets and corresponding tools. Guided by this plan, Reviso performs goal-directed active perception by selectively revisiting temporal segments and combining tools for fine-grained inspection. It interprets the acquired evidence, updates its plan as needed, and integrates global and local information to generate the final caption. To learn this observation strategy, we develop a verification-guided pipeline that constructs high-quality training trajectories through factual verification and teacher-guided refinement. We further train Reviso using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), incorporating a key-fact reward for caption quality, a Plan Alignment Reward (PAR) for identifying important observation targets, and an Unproductive Tool-Call Penalty (UTCP) that adjusts observation-cost penalties based on caption quality. Experiments across four video captioning benchmarks show that Reviso outperforms the evaluated open-source baselines, while its generated captions better support downstream video question answering. These findings highlight the effectiveness and potential of priority-guided active observation for video captioning.
items.title: Reviso: Not All Visual Evidence Deserves Equal Attention in Video Captioning

items.summary: Full Waveform Inversion (FWI) is a fundamental inverse problem in geophysics to estimate subsurface properties, such as velocity, from seismic measurements. Recently, self-supervised learning methods remove the need for ground-truth velocity maps during training by leveraging a forward operator to simulate seismic data from predictions and backpropagate the gradients of reconstruction loss through it. In this work, we consider a more challenging setting without accessing such gradients. To this end, we incorporate reinforcement learning into self-supervised FWI and propose a framework named DeepWaveRL. Specifically, we reformulate FWI as a policy learning problem, where the policy network predicts velocity maps as actions, and a forward operator is used solely for simulation. A global scalar reward is computed based on data misfit for each prediction and used to weight policy gradients. Thus, learning proceeds without accessing the gradients from the forward operator. Given the indirect and coarse supervision signals, we further identify key strategies to stabilize learning and mitigate the spatial credit assignment bottleneck. Experimental results show that, despite relying entirely on a single scalar reward, DeepWaveRL achieves competitive performance compared to supervised and self-supervised baselines. These findings suggest that our framework offers a flexible and complementary learning paradigm for the FWI research community.
items.title: DeepWaveRL: Self-Supervised Full Waveform Inversion via Reinforcement Learning

items.summary: Graph forecasters for sensor networks are trained in one regime and deployed in others, where sensor coupling and signal frequency content both change. We split this spectral shift into an operator channel and a frequency channel, each with a dimensionless measure. ST-GFM (Spectral-Temporal Graph Forecasting Model) filters every input step with Chebyshev and bidirectional diffusion filters on one learned, non-symmetric operator and alternates them with per-node temporal attention. For the operator channel we prove Frobenius-norm perturbation bounds for both graph branches, show that the Chebyshev bound is attained to first order, and compute its constant from the trained weights and the measured operator norm: 17.9 on METR-LA and 21.5 on PEMS-BAY. Under random edge dropout the trained layer moves by 2.0% to 3.1% of this bound. Masked Spectral Reconstruction (MSR), a self-supervised loss active in the first 40 epochs, matches the log power spectrum of the encoder output to that of the input. For small log-spectral residuals on unclamped bins it is proportional to an Itakura-Saito divergence to leading order. Removing it raises the 60-minute MAE by 0.30 on METR-LA, close to the 0.33 lost when all three self-supervised losses go. Under one shared evaluation pipeline, the 60-minute MAE of ST-GFM is 3.5% below a retrained STAEformer on METR-LA and 13.0% below it on PEMS-BAY. Its 60-minute MAE is 3.0980.017 on METR-LA (five seeds) and 1.5760.006 on PEMS-BAY (three seeds), the lowest PEMS-BAY MAE among twelve published baselines.
items.title: ST-GFM: Spectral-Temporal Graph Forecasting with Measured Perturbation Bounds and Masked Spectral Reconstruction

items.summary: Dataset description This dataset provides gap-filled daily, high-resolution binary snow cover maps for 12 eddy-covariance stations within the FLUXNET, ICOS, and i-Box networks distributed across the French, Swiss, Austrian, and Italian Alps. The maps were generated to characterize surface snow conditions within the source areas of eddy-covariance measurements for the updated analysis of Scheidt et al. (2026). The dataset was specifically used to determine whether the area enclosed by a station’s 80% flux-footprint contour was snow covered and to calculate the snow-cover fraction (SCF) within that footprint. Footprint-scale SCF can be calculated from the maps as the proportion of valid pixels within the footprint classified as snow covered. The data cover the following eddy-covariance sites for the hydrological years (1 st October - 30 th September) from 2013/14 to 2023/24: Alp Weissenstein (CH-Aws), Switzerland Col du Lautaret (FR-CLt), France Früebüel (CH-Fru), Switzerland Monte Bondone (IT-MBo), Italy Mazia Pasture (IT-MtP), Italy Neustift (AT-Neu), Austria Nivolet (IT-NiG), Italy Torgnon (IT-Tor), Italy The i-Box observational network in the Inn Valley, Austria, comprising the Eggen (CS-SF1), Kolsass (CS-VF0), Hochhäuser (CS-NF27), and Weerberg (CS-NF10) stations For each station outside the i-Box network, the NetCDF files cover a 15 km × 15 km square centered on the station. Because the four i-Box stations are located close to one another, they are represented by a common 20 km × 20 km domain centered on the station cluster. The maps have a spatial resolution of 50 m and are provided in the WGS 84 / UTM zone 32N coordinate reference system (EPSG:32632). Files are organized by site and hydrological year. The binary snow cover condition variable represents daily snow-cover conditions, while the reconstruction_method variable distinguishes pixels obtained from high-resolution satellite observations from pixels reconstructed by the gap-filling procedure. items.summary: Reduced-order models (ROMs) learned from trusted numerical simulations enable the real-time simulation of complex physical systems, making computationally prohibitive tasks-such as uncertainty quantification and optimal control-tractable. In particular, data-driven ROMs are opening the opportunity to learn from both numerical simulations and experimental data. However, integrating these sources of information is far from straightforward. Real-world measurements often involve multiple sources of uncertainty, including non-Gaussian noise, latent heterogeneities, unknown or hidden system parameters, and multiscale phenomena occurring below the resolution of the data. Consequently, real-world data are better described by parametrized stochastic partial differential equations, for which the development of effective ROMs remains relatively unexplored. In this work, we introduce POD-CNF, a data-driven generative ROM for efficient uncertainty quantification of parametrized high-dimensional systems. The approach combines projection-based model reduction and deep generative modeling. First, Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) is employed to obtain a low-dimensional representation of the solution manifold. A Conditional Normalizing Flow (CNF) is then trained to approximate the density of the reduced coefficients conditionally on the input parameters. This formulation allows the surrogate to capture complex, multimodal output distributions, going beyond standard regression-based ROMs and least-squares predictions. We assess the effectiveness of POD-CNF through numerical experiments, demonstrating its ability to accurately reproduce output distributions while substantially reducing computational costs. Finally, a proof-of-concept application illustrates how the generative paradigm facilitates integration into Bayesian inverse problems, highlighting promising directions for future research.
items.title: POD-CNF: reduced order modeling of parametrized stochastic PDEs via normalizing flows and proper orthogonal decomposition

items.summary: We study the local differential geometry of a Fourier-based modular-addition circuit in a one-layer transformer whose algorithm has previously been reverse-engineered. For each of the five key Fourier frequencies, we restrict the model's multilayer perceptron (MLP) contribution to a corresponding Fourier input plane and readout, and measure its directional Beltrami coefficient under continuous input perturbations. Whereas nondegenerate restrictions of ideal complex multiplication are conformal, the trained maps exhibit nonconformal distortion (median $|μ|=0.304$--$0.446$), spatial organization in the Beltrami argument, and regions of local orientation reversal. The median across frequencies decreases from $0.939$ at initialization to $0.390$ after training. The key-frequency planes also show lower median distortion than most random-plane controls, although their distributions overlap and the coordinate frames differ in conditioning. Across 500 checkpoints in one training run, most of the aggregate reduction in Beltrami magnitude occurs before the principal increase in the measured Fourier-circuit formation. At the individual-input level, Beltrami magnitude shows negligible association with the correct-logit margin ($|ρ|\leq0.026$). Late-checkpoint measurements across six runs show comparable distortion for most selected frequencies. These results provide a quantitative characterization of local deformation in a frequency-projected component of an identified neural circuit, complementary to its algorithmic reconstruction.
items.title: Nonconformal Distortion and Local Orientation Reversal in the Fourier Circuit of a Modular-Addition Transformer

items.summary: LLM agents repeatedly send a growing conversation to a model, making prefix reuse central to efficient serving. We show that a brief surge can disrupt this reuse and trigger metastable failure in prefill--decode (PD) disaggregated engines: service remains degraded after arrivals return to a load the engine previously sustained. On SGLang, a ten-minute surge reduced goodput by about 88% over the following hour. Removing the residual burst sessions restored service within minutes. The sustaining mechanism is population-cache feedback. Slower calls prolong sessions and enlarge their aggregate context, or working set; the resulting cache misses increase recomputation and further delay departures. A fluid model identifies the resource conditions for this feedback and explains how cache capacity, tool time and base load affect vulnerability. Across 36 simulated deployments, it flags all 17 cache-first cases. Controlled simulations hold the post-surge state fixed and show that changing subsequent arrivals alone reverses the recovery outcome. Once the cache collapses, low-reuse departure capacity sets the scale of the load reduction needed for recovery. Guided by these dynamics, we build Basin, which gives each session a fixed priority, reserves their predicted peak contexts against an adaptive admission budget, extends the cache with idle decode memory, and sheds excess demand. On real H200 1P3D deployments under surges, including long-context SWE-bench Pro sessions, an arrival-time prototype achieves 1.20--1.70x the goodput of Continuum and 2.35--3.59x that of HiCache alone. In simulation, the predictor-driven policy delivers 1.20--2.05x the strongest baseline's goodput across six surge scenarios.

items.summary: Unrefereed research candidate. In one sentence: the matrix geometric mean can jump at singular matrices, every possible jump is described by one rank condition, and the same mechanism refutes a published claim that the symbol of the geometric mean of two GLT matrix-sequences is always the geometric mean of their symbols. The geometric mean A#B of two positive definite matrices is the matrix analogue of √(ab), used to average covariance matrices and structured matrices and to define the Matsumoto fidelity of quantum states. It need not be continuous at singular pairs. Theorem 1 shows that X is a limit of A j #B j with positive definite A j → A, B j → B exactly when X ≽ 0, the block matrix [[A, X], [X, B]] is positive semidefinite and its rank is at most the dimension N (a dilation description with an auxiliary contraction already follows from recent work of Jones; the explicit elimination is the contribution). At equal inputs this gives the full set of limits and the exact interval of limiting Matsumoto fidelities. For generalized locally Toeplitz (GLT) matrix-sequences, uniformly bounded positive definite inputs with identical scalar symbols can have geometric means with the wrong symbol (4/5 instead of 1 on half the interval) or no eigenvalue distribution at all. This refutes Theorem 4 and Conjecture 1 of the arXiv version of Ilyas, Khan, Loi and Serra-Capizzano and, according to an AI-assisted reading of the published text, Theorem 3 and Conjecture 1 of their article in Linear Algebra Appl. (2025); the failing step of the proof is located. Positive results: closure for every Kubo-Ando mean when the sum of the symbols is positive definite almost everywhere; a one-sided theorem that the regularised symbol is always an upper envelope; and, for bounded Riemann-integrable scalar symbols of the space variable only, a sharp dichotomy (the formula holds for every realisation if and only if the symbols have no common zero set of positive measure or essentially disjoint supports). The classical two-dimensional discontinuity, Ando's maximal characterisation and the envelope X ≼ A#B are earlier work and are credited. The archive contains the manuscript (PDF and Markdown source), two figures with the script that draws them, an exact verifier (verify_exact.py, Python standard library only, 1,030 rational and Gaussian-rational checks of closed forms and finite assemblies, with a mutation self-test) and its retained output, the bibliography with its Crossref/arXiv records, the dated novelty ledger, a revision note, CI and SHA-256 sums. Assurance: written proofs; the verifier checks finite exact identities, not the theorems' limits or quantifiers; internal AI-assisted review only (not human peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification). Creator: Anonymous. Text and figures CC0-1.0; code MIT.

items.summary: We disprove a three-step error estimate for the Broyden--Fletcher--Goldfarb--Shanno {(BFGS)} method with exact line searches. We construct a globally strongly convex function $F\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and a single nonterminating trajectory $x_k\to0$ for which $\limsup_{k\to\infty}\|x_{k+3}\|/(\|x_{k+2}\|\|x_k\|)=+\infty$. The Hessian of $F$ lies between $\tfrac12 I$ and $\tfrac32 I$ everywhere, and $F(x)-\tfrac12\|x\|^2$ is compactly supported with all derivatives vanishing at $0$. The proof first constructs point-gradient pairs satisfying the exact BFGS step identities. A five-step cycle produces a large three-step quotient and restores an invariant plane for the actual updated matrix, allowing the cycle to be repeated with arbitrarily small gradient errors. Disjoint smooth corrections to a quadratic then realize all the pairs by one objective. Strong convexity identifies the prescribed points with the unique exact line-search minimizers. Thus smoothness and strong convexity do not imply the proposed product estimate, even for an objective that agrees with a quadratic to every order at its minimizer.
items.title: A counterexample to a three-step convergence bound for BFGS with exact line search

items.summary: There are many causal discovery algorithms, but few guiding principles for choosing between them. Methods are usually compared through three lenses: identifiability, consistency, and benchmarks. Each introduces assumptions about the data-generating process that are often untestable. We argue that there are no shared standards for comparing, prioritizing, or even discussing those assumptions. We support this claim by showing that (i) identifiability assumptions are often preferred by convention rather than by principle, (ii) uniform consistency requires further untestable assumptions, while the weaker pointwise consistency has arguably narrowed algorithm design, and (iii) benchmarks are not neutral tests but carry an epistemic role of their own: they quietly fix which regimes matter, which guarantees come into play, and what counts as success. In doing so, they shape what algorithm comparisons are taken to show and thus perform some of the same epistemic work as theory, but less transparently. In this position paper we argue for a more transparent, integrated practice: Make the epistemic standards for discussing identifiability and consistency assumptions explicit, especially their failure modes and scope conditions; design benchmarks to operationalize those standards, by stress-testing and ablating both. Then, theoretical and empirical results jointly clarify when, why, and how algorithms may work rather than accumulate as disconnected advances.
items.title: Causal discovery needs explicit epistemic standards

items.summary: Reliable forensic evidence extraction from mobile SQLite databases is challenging because application schemas are undocumented, evolve across releases, and differ across operating systems, making schema-specific methods brittle and difficult to maintain. We present SNEEF, a symbolic-neural framework for context-aware evidence extraction that encodes each SQLite row as context-value pairs with standardized provenance metadata and column labels, uses a language model to recognize nine forensic entity types, and binds each accepted entity to its source table and row through the PA-EEP provenance protocol. We evaluate SNEEF against examiner-verified ground truth from five corpora built from public Android and iOS device images, spanning multiple application versions. SNEEF achieves an F1 score of 0.967 for evidence entities extracted from SQLite row content, excluding application names, compared with 0.728 for a context-free configuration, with consistent gains across all corpora. We also introduce an Evidence Failure Mode taxonomy to characterize why extraction errors occur.
items.title: A Symbolic-Neural Framework for Context-Aware Evidence Extraction from Mobile SQLite Databases

items.summary: Abstract: Classical inferential statistics and p-value hypothesis testing in healthcare big data repositories suffer from severe structural limitations, notably p-hacking, asymptotic N-bias, and the frequent violation of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) assumptions due to intra-patient longitudinal dependencies, hospital clustering, and epidemiological shockwaves. To overcome these failures, we introduce an Inverse Breakpoint Analysis, a scale-invariant, physics-inspired metrological audit framework. Our analysis treats discrete clinical event counts not as abstract probabilities, but as physical informational mass. Grounded in Garwood exact discrete limits and Wilson-Hilferty approximations, the framework extends our previous work on stress testing indices for Big health data and establishes three rigorous thresholds: a pure mass saturation limit, a baseline tolerance band, and a structural signal threshold. Through the use of these three parameters, our inverse breakpoint analysis eliminates false-positive artifacts induced by massive repository sizes while preventing under-powering in small cohorts. Ultimately, the framework demonstrates that percentage-based thresholds are kinematic artifacts of scale, whereas absolute excess discrete mass serves as the sole physical invariant for healthcare data validation. We validated this approach with numerous illustrative examples.
items.title: Inverse Breakpoint Analysis: A Scale-Invariant Physics-Inspired Metrological Audit for Sanitary Big Data

items.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves the single-sample quality of visual generative models, but deployment often provides additional inference compute through Best-of-N sampling. Whether RL gains transfer under such test-time scaling, particularly on difficult held-out tasks, remains poorly understood in the visual domain. Our central contribution is to systematically identify and characterize a failure mode of scaling transfer in visual RL: across multiple RL methods, model backbones, and evaluations spanning compositional generation, text rendering, and preference alignment, higher single-sample reward does not necessarily imply a better quality-compute frontier. RL gains may attenuate, saturate, or even reverse at large sampling budgets, with the base model eventually outperforming its post-trained counterpart. We explain these regimes through a quantile-transfer framework, showing that Best-of-N places increasing weight on the upper tail of the reward distribution as N grows. Consequently, RL can improve typical samples while compressing or degrading the rare high-quality outcomes that test-time scaling exploits. As a simple intervention motivated by this analysis, we introduce Quantile Utility Policy Optimization (QUPO), which optimizes a controllable mixture of quantile utilities corresponding to different inference budgets. Experiments on SD3.5-M and BAGEL show that QUPO better preserves upper-tail quality and substantially improves scaling on challenging held-out prompts relative to standard RL post-training. Our results suggest that visual generative models should be evaluated and optimized not only for single-sample quality, but for how post-training reshapes the full reward distribution that inference-time scaling exploits.
items.title: Do Visual RL Gains Scale at Test Time? A Quantile View of Post-Training

items.summary: Memory systems for LLM agents are evaluated mostly on social dialogue, where facts accumulate and rarely change, so remembering reduces largely to finding the turn in which something was said. Financial dialogue breaks this assumption: figures are revised, stances shift without being restated, rules stated once govern later questions, and a single company is discussed under several analytical lenses. Memory systems that retrieve the passages most similar to a question, or the most recent ones, therefore return superseded values, miss rules that share no wording with the question, and cannot recover a stance spread across sessions. We present TrackMem, a per-speaker graph memory that tracks the history of figures, separates perspectives by entity and lens, and preserves each speaker's actions in chronological order. To evaluate it, we introduce FinLoCoMo, a benchmark of 15 long-horizon investment conversations with 765 questions in two splits: one following the LoCoMo categories and one targeting four failure modes. With two readers, TrackMem outperforms existing memory systems on both splits. On the failure-mode split it reaches 73.9% macro accuracy against 69.4% for the strongest baseline, with the largest gains on questions about revised figures (86.5% against 73.4%).
items.title: TrackMem: Tracking Evolving Beliefs in Long-Horizon Financial Dialogue

items.summary: The self-controlled case series (SCCS) design is widely used in studies of rare events, for example of vaccine side effects. Conceptually, the design has two main features. First, it requires only data from individuals who have experienced the event of interest. Therefore, the design is especially useful when the outcome is rare and the available data come from surveillance or clinical records, say, of hospitalized patients. Second, because comparisons are made within single individuals, time-invariant confounding between treatment and outcome is eliminated. We formulate a set of sufficient identification assumptions for estimating the causal effect of vaccination on an adverse outcome under the SCCS design, drawing on ideas from the causal inference literature. Unlike the existing SCCS literature, we do not consider a parametric model as the starting point. This allows us to establish when and why the SCCS design allows identification of causal effects, using data from cases only. However, because the sufficient identifiability assumptions are implausible in some applications, we also develop statistical tests for the existence of a treatment effect that remain valid when only a subset of the identification assumptions holds.
items.title: Causal Inference from Self-controlled Case Series

items.summary: Optimal control of partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs), in general, requires a complete history. The belief state, a distribution over hidden states, summarizes this history and provides the classical sufficient statistic to control POMDPs. However, the continuous nature of the belief space generally prevents a finite-memory controller from maintaining it exactly. This raises the question we address in this work: what must the available finite memory preserve to achieve near-optimal control performance? We study this question through an information-theoretic converse that gives a fundamental lower bound on the loss of any finite-memory controller. The analysis introduces the concept of a decision witness that characterizes belief states whose confusion would lead to unavoidable loss. Motivated by this bound, we propose RECAP, a constructive quantization method for designing representative memory states. We prove an upper bound on the optimality gap of any RECAP codebook and use the components of this bound together with the converse analysis to define the codebook objective. Experiments on 11 POMDP benchmarks demonstrate that RECAP improves over finite-memory representation baselines under the same memory budget.
items.title: Finite-Memory Control of POMDPs: Fundamental Limits and Efficient Design

items.summary: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization has emerged as a promising approach for memory-efficient large language model (LLM) post-training, yet its reliable application to reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) remains largely unexplored. Motivated by the distinct data regimes of on-policy RL and fixed-data optimization, we develop a generic variance-theoretic framework to investigate what limits the reliability of ZO gradient estimation. Our analysis reveals that estimation reliability is structurally determined by whether the two finite-difference evaluations are performed on matched data. On-policy reinforcement learning (RL) under the mismatched-data regime produces a $1/μ^2$ oracle-noise amplification that sets an irreducible noise floor as the perturbation scale $μ$ decreases, whereas Boltzmann Targeted SFT (BOLT) under the matched-data regime eliminates this amplification via noise cancellation. We further derive convergence guarantees with explicit constants that cleanly separate the two regimes. These results naturally lead to ZO-BOLT, which applies ZO optimization to BOLT's RLVR-aligned weighted-SFT objective. Controlled perturbation-scale sweeps and matched-versus-mismatched end-to-end comparisons validate the predicted effect of data matching. Experiments across three model variants and two mathematical reasoning benchmarks further show that ZO-BOLT consistently improves over the pretrained baseline while retaining a near-inference memory footprint. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/lianmin-chen/the_cost_of_mismatch.
items.title: The Cost of Mismatch: Noise Amplification in Zeroth-Order Reinforcement Learning

items.summary: Visual mental imagery (VMI) decoding uses brain activity to reconstruct internally generated visual scenes, providing a potential pathway for externalizing internal experiences and developing neuroprosthetic communication interfaces. However, progress is limited by the lack of dedicated, training-scale VMI datasets. Current VMI paradigms often rely on visual prompts or short-term memory images, introducing visual and mnemonic confounds that make it difficult to disentangle neural activity associated with endogenous image construction from signals driven by prior or concurrent visual input. Furthermore, existing VMI datasets offer limited descriptive control over individual visual attributes, making it difficult to systematically assess fine grained visual details. To address these gaps, we introduce AVID, the first dedicated training-scale 5.0 Tesla functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) resource for auditory-induced VMI decoding. AVID comprises approximately 67 hours of dense recordings from nine participants. The dataset is structured into two complementary splits: a scene-level complex split using naturalistic Mandarin descriptions and a controlled simple split with explicitly specified visual attributes. We further formalize a standardized evaluation protocol that decouples source-image consistency from semantic alignment, allowing for a more nuanced assessment of imagery reconstruction. Baseline qualitative and quantitative results show that current reconstruction pipelines remain limited on AVID, although the most successful reconstructions preserve recognizable scene level semantics from spoken descriptions. By combining dedicated training-scale neural recordings and standardized evaluation resources, AVID provides both a data foundation for imagery-specific model development and a benchmark for evaluating VMI decoding with substantially reduced sensory contamination.
items.title: AVID: A 5T fMRI Dataset for Benchmarking Auditory-induced Visual Mental Imagery Decoding

items.summary: The Sundarbans mangrove system constitutes a globally consequential blue carbon sink, yet vertically resolved soil organic carbon (SOC) inventories, particularly at depth, remain under-constrained. This study deployed a geospatial deep-learning pipeline integrating multi-source Earth observation data (optical, SAR, and DEM-derived covariates) to spatially upscale SOC stocks to 1 m depth across the Bangladesh Sundarbans. Stratified coring across five sites positioned along the salinity–tidal inundation gradient to represent four major vegetation zones (n = 25; one pit per site × five depth intervals: 0–20, 20–40, 40–60, 60–80, 80–100 cm) captured physicochemical and SOC attributions. A Kruskal–Wallis test confirmed a positive SOC gradient with depth (H = 21.7, df = 4, p < 0.001); post-hoc Dunn’s pairwise comparisons showed 60–100 cm layers differed significantly from all shallower layers (p < 0.01, Bonferroni-adjusted), with the dominant pool residing below 40 cm, implying systematic underestimation by conventional shallow-core (<30–40 cm) assessments. To partition total ecosystem carbon and establish soil-pool dominance, above- and belowground biomass were parameterized using species-specific allometric equations, revealing high stem density but comparatively low basal area consistent with a regenerating stand structure dominated by Heritiera fomes and Sonneratia apetala. Analysis of a previously published Landsat-derived mangrove record (1988–2022) revealed net contraction in mangrove extent; loss-agent raster attribution, based on shoreline-proximity buffers, land-cover transition sequences and cyclone-track coincidence, identified chronic tidal abrasion and erosion as the primary driver rather than anthropogenic conversion or cyclonic disturbance. Benchmarking against a previously published global 30 m machine-learning SOC product revealed a 4.2-fold underestimation of SOC stocks in the Bangladesh Sundarbans, particularly in peat-enriched, anoxic substrata. Assimilation of deep-profile in situ observations with the pipeline significantly improves spatial prediction fidelity and establishes a robust baseline for Measurement, Reporting, and Verification for greenhouse gas inventories, highlighting the necessity of incorporating deep-soil carbon pools for inventorizing erosion-vulnerable seaward margins.
